surfaces.part: striped orange and white awning plane
cream front wall or counter face with valance

answer.evidence: Rows 3-7 are an orange and white striped awning, a sloped canopy plane. Its lowest row 7 is darker orange and acts as eave shadow. Row 8 is a dark 1-row edge line below it. Below that, rows 9-13 are a cream and tan front face, and rows 14-15 are a dark and white base, giving about 7 front rows. Rows 0-2 are a front-facing dark and tan cornice strip with no top surface, which is not counted. The awning gives a top of 5 rows above a front face of 3+ rows, so it reads as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny fragment, roughly one or two tiles, that reads as a striped orange-and-white awning over a small sign or counter. It is not a whole building with roof, walls, door and windows like the references, so the kind does not match. Measured facts: 9 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels. That suggests tinted outlines rather than a black sticker line, but the whole piece uses only 9 colours in total, against 185 and 66 for the references. By eye, the awning stripes are simple bands of about 3 lightness steps (light, mid, dark) with no per-tile scallops, plaster speckle or grain like the references' roof tiles and stone. The piece has fewer steps and less texture than the references, so it would look flatter and thinner beside them. Because it is not the same kind and is shallower, I fail it, as the instructions say to when in doubt.

answer.evidence: Rows 3-7 are the awning plane, with alternating white and orange stripes. The orange columns darken at row 7 (#b4552c), and row 8 is a dark scalloped edge line (#383c58) that serves as the front-edge line, so the awning counts as a canopy top surface (evidence c). Below it, rows 9-13 show a cream front face with a tan band at row 10, and rows 14-15 are a dark line and a white base. Rows 0-2 are a front-facing dark/tan/dark cornice strip with no edge line or shadow, so I did not count it as a top. The awning stripes run vertically, which makes the top reading somewhat weak, but the edge line and shading are enough to call it three_quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny awning or sign fragment, about 16x12 source pixels, with an orange and white striped top and a pale grey base bar. It is not a whole building with roof, walls and door or windows, so it does not match the reference kind. Overall it looks thinner and more sticker-like than the references, and it does not show the structural depth of a Beodeul building.
